name: Firebase Blaze
tagline: Provide a local emulator-backed backend for one app without recreating Google's global services

pricing.notes: Blaze is pay as you go; canonical monthly amount is null.

tiers.name: Spark
tiers.limits: Auth 50,000 MAU; Firestore 1 GiB, 50,000 reads/day, 20,000 writes/day and 20,000 deletes/day; Hosting 10 GB storage and 10 GB transfer/month; Realtime Database 1 GB, 100 concurrent connections and 10 GB download/month.
tiers.notes: Test Lab includes 10 virtual-device and 5 physical-device tests/day; exceeding hard Spark limits generally stops the affected service rather than billing.

tiers.name: Blaze
tiers.limits: No base fee; retains no-cost quotas and adds Functions 2M invocations/month, 400,000 GB-seconds, 200,000 CPU-seconds and 5 GB egress; then pay as you go.
tiers.notes: Realtime Database supports up to 200,000 simultaneous connections/database; exact rates vary by product and region.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Spark: Auth 50,000 MAU; Firestore 1 GiB plus 50,000 reads/day and 20,000 writes/day; Hosting 10 GB storage plus 10 GB transfer/month; Realtime Database 1 GB and 100 concurrent connections
pricing.billingTerms: Spark is free with hard caps; Blaze has $0 base and monthly pay-as-you-go billing; no annual plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: Blaze bills every Firebase/Google Cloud product independently after free quotas. Budget alerts do not stop spend, Storage pricing follows Google Cloud by region, and enabling Blaze can make previously hard-stopped usage billable.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Firebase Blaze, provide a local emulator-backed backend for one app without recreating Google's global services. The hard boundary is global database, auth, push, analytics, serverless, mobile sdks, and operations, plus infrastructure scale, operations, and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Provide a local emulator-backed backend for one app on a user-owned server, route domains, retain logs, and perform backups without recreating Google's global services.
whatYouLose: global database, auth, push, analytics, serverless, mobile SDKs, and operations
ongoingBurden: patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Firebase Blaze because hosting products sell an operations team and failure-domain diversity, not merely a deploy button. The recurring cost buys patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Coolify
priorArt.desc: Active open-source self-hosting platform for applications, databases, and services.

alternatives.name: Appwrite
alternatives.desc: Auth, database, storage, realtime, and functions behind one polished console; the Compose file is doing a lot.

facts.install: Hosted Appwrite Cloud signup, or the official Docker installer/Compose stack
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted Appwrite stores application records in MariaDB, queues and cache in Redis, and uploaded files in Docker volumes or a configured object-storage adapter; functions and build artifacts are managed by the Appwrite worker/executor services. Appwrite Cloud stores the equivalent data in Appwrite's infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: Appwrite covers auth, data, files, functions, and realtime, but it lacks Firebase's mature offline mobile SDKs, global managed scale, Analytics, Crashlytics, Messaging, and Google ecosystem.
facts.setupBlocker: The installer is one command, but it expands into a large multi-container platform; production use still needs a domain, TLS, SMTP, storage, backups, and careful version upgrades.

alternatives.name: Nhost
alternatives.desc: Postgres plus GraphQL, auth, storage, functions, and realtime; closer to Firebase than most Firebase alternatives.

facts.install: Hosted Nhost project, or Nhost CLI/Docker for local and self-hosted deployments
facts.dataFormat: Application and auth records live in PostgreSQL, GraphQL metadata and migrations can live beside the project in version-controlled files, uploaded objects use S3-compatible storage, and serverless-function source remains in the project directory. Nhost Cloud runs those services in Nhost's infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: Nhost replaces Firebase with PostgreSQL and GraphQL, but gives up Firestore's offline-first client behavior, Google mobile services, global operational footprint, and breadth of first-party SDKs.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting means operating PostgreSQL, Hasura, authentication, storage, functions, networking, secrets, email, and upgrades rather than one small binary.

alternatives.name: PocketBase
alternatives.desc: For one modest app, a single local binary covers data, auth, files, realtime, and an admin UI; functions are the missing piece.

facts.install: Download one platform binary and run `pocketbase serve`; build from Go source only for custom extensions
facts.dataFormat: Collections, auth records, settings, and application data live in SQLite files under `pb_data`; uploaded files live under `pb_data/storage` by default or in configured S3-compatible storage, and schema migrations can be kept as JavaScript files in `pb_migrations`.
facts.gapVsPaid: PocketBase is excellent for one modest app, but a single SQLite server with no built-in functions runtime cannot match Firebase's offline SDKs, global scaling, messaging, analytics, or managed operations.
facts.setupBlocker: It installs unusually cleanly, but a public deployment still needs process supervision, HTTPS/reverse proxying, backups of `pb_data`, and a deliberate upgrade routine.

alternatives.name: Supabase
alternatives.desc: A local, self-hosted backend with emulators-by-Docker: database, auth, storage, realtime, functions, and APIs.

facts.install: Hosted Supabase project, or the official Docker Compose stack; `supabase start` runs the local stack
facts.dataFormat: Relational data, auth records, and platform metadata live in PostgreSQL; Realtime consumes the Postgres replication stream; object data lives in the configured storage backend with metadata in Postgres; edge-function and migration source stays in project files. Supabase Cloud stores and operates the managed copy.
facts.gapVsPaid: Supabase is the broadest substitute, but Firebase still has the tighter mobile SDK, offline sync, Analytics, Crashlytics, Cloud Messaging, Remote Config, and Google-service integration.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting is not 'just Postgres': the Compose stack needs many secrets and services, plus SMTP, object storage, TLS, backups, observability, and coordinated upgrades.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Blaze plan and a single-server personal platform DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Firebase Blaze in an empty repository.
Use Docker Compose, Caddy, PostgreSQL, Redis, and a small Go control plane; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: provide a local emulator-backed backend for one app on a user-owned server, route domains, retain logs, and perform backups without recreating Google's global services.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Accept a Git repository or container image and one explicit Dockerfile-based build path.
Implement applications, environments, secrets, domains, health checks, and rolling container replacement.
Use Caddy for automatic TLS and route only to healthy local containers.
Capture bounded build and runtime logs and expose restart, rollback, and redeploy actions.
Back up PostgreSQL metadata and document backups for each deployed application's data volumes.
Add host metrics, disk alerts, update instructions, disaster recovery, and a prominent single-server warning.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out multi-region or serverless infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out managed data stores and global edge delivery.
Deliberately leave out DDoS response, compliance, and guaranteed uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
